items.q: Which sentence best captures the conclusion?
choices: Scheduling should target the forgetting edge, not comfort.
Input volume matters more than review.
items.a: Scheduling should target the forgetting edge, not comfort.

passage: Most learners judge their progress by how smoothly a study session feels. The evidence points the other way. When you review material you half remember, the effort of pulling it back into focus strengthens the memory far more than rereading ever does. Psychologists call this the testing effect, and it survives almost every attempt to kill it in the lab. Spacing amplifies it: the longer you intend to remember something, the longer the gap between reviews should be. Difficulty, in the right dose at the right moment, is not the enemy of learning. It is the mechanism. The catch is that effortful practice feels worse while it happens, which is exactly why so many learners drift back to comfortable, ineffective habits. A good system does not ask how the session felt. It schedules review at the edge of forgetting and lets the results speak a month later.
